cells.html:
Astronomical objects often fall into groups that we do not know in advance. Examples are the types of galaxies and the stellar populations of a globular cluster. Clustering divides a set of objects into such groups using only their features.

Clustering differs from the classification of Chapter 7. A classifier learns the boundaries between classes from objects whose classes are known, which is supervised learning. Clustering is unsupervised learning, so it uses no labels and looks at the data itself to find groups. This suits discovery science, where we may not know which categories to expect. Figure 11.1 compares the two tasks.

Clustering has three advantages in astronomy. It needs no preconceived categories, so it can reveal unexpected structure. It handles catalogs that are too large for manual classification. It can also find finer differences than the traditional schemes that astronomers developed by visual inspection.

Clustering also has difficulties, because evaluating results without ground truth labels is more subjective than in supervised learning. The number of clusters often depends on the scientific question as well as on the data. Different algorithms can give different clusters for the same data, so we must know their assumptions.

Clustering rests on a simple premise, that similar objects probably belong to the same group and dissimilar objects to different groups. Different definitions of similarity lead to different algorithms.

K-means defines similarity as the distance to a cluster center, which is a geometric view. Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) describe the data with a probability distribution and give each object a probability of belonging to each cluster.

11.1 Mathematical Formulation of K-means

K-means divides the data into \(K\) groups by assigning each data point to the group with the nearest center.

Let the data set consist of \(N\) observations \(\{\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_N\}\), where each \(\mathbf{x}_i\) is a \(D\)-dimensional feature vector. In a study of stellar populations, the features can be the metallicity and the carbon and nitrogen abundances measured from spectra.

K-means finds \(K\) cluster centers \(\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_1, \boldsymbol{\mu}_2, \ldots, \boldsymbol{\mu}_K\}\) and assigns each data point to one cluster. The binary indicator \(r_{ik} \in \{0, 1\}\) records the assignment, with \(r_{ik} = 1\) if \(\mathbf{x}_i\) belongs to cluster \(k\) and \(r_{ik} = 0\) otherwise.

The values \(r_{i1}\) to \(r_{iK}\) of a point form the one-hot encoding of Chapter 8, with a single entry equal to 1. For \(K=3\) clusters and a data point \(\mathbf{x}_5\) in cluster 2, we have \(r_{51} = 0\), \(r_{52} = 1\) and \(r_{53} = 0\). Each point belongs to one cluster, so \(\sum_{k=1}^K r_{ik} = 1\) for all \(i\).

The K-means Objective Function

The goal of K-means is to find centers and assignments that make the clusters as compact as possible. We measure compactness by the sum of squared distances between each data point and its assigned center \[ J = \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K r_{ik} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2. \]

The quantity \(\|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2\) is the squared Euclidean distance between \(\mathbf{x}_i\) and \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\). The factor \(r_{ik}\) selects only the distance to the assigned center, because \(r_{ik} = 1\) for one \(k\) only. Each data point therefore adds one squared distance to \(J\). A smaller \(J\) means that the points lie closer to their centers, so the clusters are more compact. The Euclidean distance depends on the units of the features. For features with different units, such as colors and morphological indices, we first rescale each feature, for example by its standard deviation (Chapter 10).

The Joint Optimization Problem

The optimization problem is \[ \min_{\{r_{ik}\}, \{\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\}} J = \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K r_{ik} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2 \] subject to \(r_{ik} \in \{0, 1\}\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^K r_{ik} = 1\) for all \(i\).

In regression and classification we optimized one set of parameters. Here we must optimize two sets of variables at once, the cluster centers \(\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\}\) and the assignments \(\{r_{ik}\}\).

The two sets of variables have a circular dependency. If we knew the optimal centers, the best assignments would be easy, because each point goes to its nearest center. If we knew the optimal assignments, finding the best centers would be easy, because each center would be the mean of its assigned points. Figure 11.2 shows the two sets of variables and the distances that enter \(J\).

This circular dependency makes direct optimization difficult. The binary constraint on \(r_{ik}\) adds a combinatorial problem. For \(N\) points and \(K\) clusters there are \(K^N\) possible assignments, a number that grows exponentially with \(N\).

The problem has \(N \times K\) binary assignment variables and \(K \times D\) continuous center coordinates. An exhaustive search over all assignments is too expensive for data sets of realistic size. Gradient descent does not work either, because the binary nature of \(r_{ik}\) prevents the use of continuous optimization techniques.

11.2 Expectation-Maximization for K-means

We can break the circular dependency by alternating between optimizing one set of variables with the other fixed. This is the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm. It turns the problem into a sequence of simpler problems that have closed-form solutions.

The procedure is a coordinate descent. It moves alternately along the assignment variables and along the center coordinates. Each step minimizes \(J\) over one set of variables, so \(J\) decreases or stays the same.

The EM algorithm for K-means has four steps.

  • Choose \(K\) initial cluster centers \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\). Random data points are a simple choice, though more sophisticated strategies often work better.

  • The E-step fixes the centers \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) and finds the optimal assignments \(r_{ik}\).

  • The M-step fixes the assignments \(r_{ik}\) and finds the optimal centers \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\).

  • Repeat the E-step and the M-step until convergence.

The algorithm has converged when the E-step changes no assignment. The names of the steps come from the mixture view of Section 11.6, where the E-step computes expected assignments and the M-step maximizes a log-likelihood. For K-means, maximizing the log-likelihood means minimizing \(J\) (Section 11.4).

The Expectation Step

In the E-step the centers \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) are fixed, and we minimize \(J\) over the assignments \[ \min_{\{r_{ik}\}} J = \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K r_{ik} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2 \] subject to \(r_{ik} \in \{0, 1\}\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^K r_{ik} = 1\) for all \(i\).

With fixed centers the problem is simple, because for each data point we choose which cluster it belongs to. Point \(\mathbf{x}_i\) belongs to one cluster, so one \(r_{ik}\) equals 1 and the others are 0. Its contribution to the objective is \[ \sum_{k=1}^K r_{ik} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2 = \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{k^*}\|^2, \] where \(k^*\) is the cluster of point \(i\).

This contribution is smallest when \(k^*\) is the index of the center closest to \(\mathbf{x}_i\). The optimal assignment is therefore \[ r_{ik} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } k = \arg\min_{j} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j\|^2 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} .\end{cases} \]The E-step therefore assigns each data point to its nearest center.

The Maximization Step

In the M-step the assignments \(r_{ik}\) are fixed, and we minimize \(J\) over the centers \[ \min_{\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\}} J = \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K r_{ik} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2. \]With fixed assignments we group the terms of the sum by cluster \[ J = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{i=1}^N r_{ik} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2 = \sum_{k=1}^K J_k, \] where \(J_k = \sum_{i=1}^N r_{ik} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2\) is the contribution of cluster \(k\).

Each \(J_k\) depends only on \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\), so we optimize each center independently. For cluster \(k\) we minimize \[ J_k = \sum_{i=1}^N r_{ik} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2. \]

Setting the gradient with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) to zero gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial J_k}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}_k} &= \sum_{i=1}^N r_{ik} \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}_k} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2\\ &= \sum_{i=1}^N r_{ik} (-2)(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)\\ &= -2 \sum_{i=1}^N r_{ik} \mathbf{x}_i + 2 \boldsymbol{\mu}_k \sum_{i=1}^N r_{ik} = 0. \end{aligned}\]Solving for \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) gives \[ \boldsymbol{\mu}_k = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N r_{ik} \mathbf{x}_i}{\sum_{i=1}^N r_{ik}}. \]The optimal center is the mean, or centroid, of the points assigned to the cluster. The denominator \(\sum_{i=1}^N r_{ik}\) counts these points, because \(r_{ik}\) is 1 for assigned points and 0 otherwise. Figure 11.3 shows how the E-step and the M-step alternate.

The Local Minima Problem

The EM algorithm converges to a solution, but it typically reaches a local minimum of \(J\) rather than the global minimum. Each step improves \(J\) only given the current state, so it gives no guarantee of global optimality. The final solution therefore depends on the initial centers. Poor starting positions can leave the algorithm in a configuration where no step lowers \(J\), although much better solutions exist. Since the cluster structure is often unknown, we need initialization methods that raise the chance of a good solution and speed up convergence.

Random Initialization

The simplest strategy picks \(K\) data points uniformly at random as the initial centers. It is easy to implement, but it can give poor solutions when centers start too close together or in regions of low data density. Figure 11.4 compares a good and a poor initialization. Running K-means several times from different random starts and keeping the result with the smallest \(J\) reduces the chance of a poor solution.

K-means++ Initialization

K-means++ has five steps and reduces the chance of poor starting centers by weighted random sampling that tends to spread them over the data.

  • Choose the first center \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_1\) uniformly at random from the data points \[ \boldsymbol{\mu}_1 \in \{\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_N\} \text{ with probability } \frac{1}{N}. \]

  • For each data point \(\mathbf{x}_i\), compute the distance \(\delta(\mathbf{x}_i)\) to the nearest chosen center \[ \delta(\mathbf{x}_i) = \min_{j \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_j\|, \] where \(m\) counts the chosen centers.

  • Choose the next center \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m+1}\) from the data points with probability proportional to \(\delta(\mathbf{x}_i)^2\) \[ P(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{m+1} = \mathbf{x}_i) = \frac{\delta(\mathbf{x}_i)^2}{\sum_{j=1}^N \delta(\mathbf{x}_j)^2}. \]

  • Repeat the previous two steps until \(K\) centers are chosen.

  • Run the standard K-means EM algorithm from these initial centers.

The squared distance gives a high probability to points far from the existing centers, so the new centers tend to spread over the data. Centers that are far from each other are less likely to lie in the same cluster. Sampling only from the data points places the centers in regions of high data density. Figure 11.5 shows the probabilities and the chosen centers for three clusters.

11.3 Evaluating K-means Clustering

Cost per Iteration

The E-step computes the distance between each of the \(N\) points and each of the \(K\) centers. Each distance needs of the order of \(D\) operations, written \(\mathcal{O}(D)\) (Section 10.8), so the E-step needs \(\mathcal{O}(NKD)\) operations.

The M-step averages the points of each cluster. Assuming roughly equal-sized clusters, each center uses about \(N/K\) points. Each mean needs \(\mathcal{O}(ND/K)\) operations, so all centers need \(\mathcal{O}(ND)\).

The E-step dominates, so one iteration costs \(\mathcal{O}(NKD)\). The cost grows linearly with the number of points, clusters and dimensions. K-means is therefore practical for astronomical data sets with millions of objects and hundreds of features. The results are also easy to interpret.

Although K-means is fast, it needs the number of clusters \(K\) in advance. The true cluster structure is usually unknown. How do we choose an appropriate value? In astronomy this asks how many types of galaxies exist or how many stellar populations a globular cluster contains.

Inertia and the Elbow Method

The most direct approach is to watch the K-means objective as \(K\) increases. The within-cluster sum of squares, or inertia, is the value of \(J\) after convergence. It measures how tightly clustered the points are \[ \text{Inertia} = \sum_{k=1}^K \sum_{i \in C_k} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2, \] where \(C_k\) is the set of points in cluster \(k\).

As \(K\) increases, the inertia decreases, because the clusters become smaller and more compact. Suppose the data contain \(K^*\) clusters. For \(K < K^*\) each added cluster separates a real group and lowers the inertia by a large amount. For \(K > K^*\) the added clusters split groups that are already compact, so the inertia falls only slowly.

We plot the inertia against \(K\) and look for the elbow, the point where the slope changes sharply. The elbow gives a candidate value of \(K\). The choice is subjective when no clear elbow exists. The elbow plot is used like the scree plot of Chapter 10, whose elbow suggests the number of principal components. Panels (a) to (c) of Figure 11.6 show an example with four clusters.

Silhouette Analysis

The silhouette score is a more quantitative approach. It measures how similar a point is to its own cluster compared with the other clusters. For point \(i\) the silhouette score is \[ s(i) = \frac{b(i) - a(i)}{\max\{a(i), b(i)\}}, \] where \(a(i)\) is the mean distance from point \(i\) to the other points of its cluster. The value \(b(i)\) is the minimum average distance between point \(i\) and the points of any other cluster.

The score lies between \(-1\) and 1. A value \(s(i) \approx 1\) means that the point is well clustered and far from the neighboring clusters. A value near 0 means that the point lies near a boundary between clusters. A value near \(-1\) means that the point may be in the wrong cluster.

We choose the \(K\) with the highest average silhouette score over all data points, as panel (d) of Figure 11.6 shows.

11.4 K-means as a Generative Model

So far we have described K-means as a geometric optimization problem. It also has a statistical interpretation, which connects K-means to probabilistic models. This connection helps explain the behavior of K-means and points toward clustering methods with fewer restrictions.

In Chapter 7 we distinguished discriminative models, which learn decision boundaries directly, from generative models, which describe how the data of each class are produced. K-means takes the generative view and applies it to the unsupervised setting, where the class labels are unknown.

In this view, the observed data come from a mixture of different underlying processes, and each cluster represents one such process. Our goal is to identify both the processes (the cluster parameters) and which process generated each data point (its cluster assignment).

A Probabilistic Data-Generating Story

We can describe K-means by a generative model with two steps. First, one of the \(K\) clusters, say cluster \(k\), is selected with equal probability \(1/K\). Then a data point is drawn from a Gaussian distribution with spherical covariance \(\sigma^2\mathrm{Id}\) around the cluster center \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\). Here \(\mathrm{Id}\) is the identity matrix, so the variance is the same in all directions.

The likelihood of data point \(\mathbf{x}_i\) is \[ p(\mathbf{x}_i) = \sum_{k=1}^K \frac{1}{K} \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \sigma^2\mathrm{Id}), \] where \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma})\) denotes the Gaussian probability density.

From Soft to Hard Assignments

The likelihood above describes soft assignment, because each data point has some probability of belonging to each cluster. K-means uses hard assignments, in which each point belongs to one cluster.

We connect the two views by putting the binary assignment variables \(r_{ik}\) into the likelihood. For hard assignments the joint probability of \(\mathbf{x}_i\) and its assignment becomes \[ p(\mathbf{x}_i, \{r_{ik}\}) = \sum_{k=1}^K r_{ik} \frac{1}{K} \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \sigma^2\mathrm{Id}). \]For each data point one \(r_{ik}\) equals 1 and the others are 0. The sum therefore reduces to the term of the assigned cluster.

For all data points, the log-likelihood is \[ \ln L = \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K r_{ik} \ln \left(\frac{1}{K} \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \sigma^2\mathrm{Id})\right). \]

Deriving the K-means Objective

Maximizing this log-likelihood over the assignments \(r_{ik}\) and the centers \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) gives the K-means objective. The Gaussian density with spherical covariance is \[ \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}, \sigma^2\mathrm{Id}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{D/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{\|\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right). \]Its logarithm is \[ \ln \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}, \sigma^2\mathrm{Id}) = -\frac{D}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{\|\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}\|^2}{2\sigma^2}. \]

Substituting into the log-likelihood gives \[\begin{aligned} \ln L &= \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K r_{ik} \left[\ln\frac{1}{K} -\frac{D}{2}\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) - \frac{\|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right]. \end{aligned}\]The first two terms are constants with respect to the assignments \(r_{ik}\) and the centers \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\), because \(\sum_{k=1}^K r_{ik} = 1\). We ignore them when we maximize the log-likelihood and keep \[ \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K r_{ik} \left[- \frac{\|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right]. \]Maximizing this expression is equivalent to minimizing \[ \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K r_{ik} \|\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k\|^2. \]This is the K-means objective, because the constant factor \(1/(2\sigma^2)\) multiplies all terms equally and does not change the optimization.

Understanding K-means Assumptions

From this derivation we see that K-means corresponds to a specific generative model with three restrictive assumptions. The clusters are spherical, because all have the same covariance matrix \(\sigma^2\mathrm{Id}\). The clusters have equal weights, because all have the prior probability \(1/K\). The assignments are hard, because each data point belongs to one cluster.

These assumptions explain both the efficiency of K-means and its limits. The spherical assumption makes the algorithm fast but restricts the clusters to roughly round shapes. It also makes the boundary between two clusters a hyperplane, a straight line in two dimensions, as in logistic regression (Chapter 7). Such a boundary cannot separate the two curved clusters of Figure 11.7, because each K-means cluster is a convex region. A region is convex when the straight segment between any two of its points stays inside it, and a half-moon is not convex.

The equal weight assumption works well when the clusters have similar populations but fails when the populations differ a lot. The hard assignment assumption provides mathematical simplicity but loses information about uncertainty in borderline cases. K-means is also sensitive to outliers, and it works best for well-separated clusters.

We can relax these assumptions by allowing different covariance matrices, different weights and soft assignments. This gives the Gaussian mixture models of the next section.

11.5 Mathematical Formulation of Gaussian Mixture Models

K-means assigns each data point to one cluster. GMMs use soft assignments, in which each data point has a probability of belonging to each cluster.

In astronomy the boundaries between populations are often fuzzy. Stars near the boundary between the disk and the halo, for example, can share the properties of both populations. Figure 11.8 shows soft assignment for three overlapping clusters.

The Mixture Model

A GMM describes the distribution of the data as a weighted sum of simpler component distributions, and each component describes one cluster. We assume that the data come from a mixture of \(K\) Gaussian distributions \[ p(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k). \]The function \(\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)\) is the multivariate Gaussian density of component \(k\), with mean vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) and covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k\). It gives the density of observing \(\mathbf{x}\) if the data point came from component \(k\). The mixture weight \(\pi_k\) is the prior probability that a randomly selected data point belongs to component \(k\). The weights satisfy \(\pi_k \geq 0\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k = 1\).

The weights are the relative abundances of the components in the population. In a galaxy survey, for example, \(\pi_1\) could be the fraction of spiral galaxies and \(\pi_2\) the fraction of elliptical galaxies. Figure 11.9 shows three components with different weights.

Increased Model Flexibility

K-means assumes the same spherical covariance for all clusters. A GMM gives each component its own covariance matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k\), called a full covariance matrix. It can therefore describe clusters with different shapes, sizes and orientations.

This flexibility needs more parameters. A GMM with \(K\) components in \(D\) dimensions has \(K-1\) free mixture weights, because the weights sum to 1. It has \(KD\) mean parameters and \(K \cdot D(D+1)/2\) covariance parameters, because each symmetric covariance matrix has \(D(D+1)/2\) free parameters. The total is \((K-1) + KD + K \cdot D(D+1)/2\) parameters, which grows quadratically with \(D\). This rapid growth can make GMMs computationally challenging in high-dimensional spaces.

Constraining Covariance Complexity

We can constrain the covariance matrices to reduce the number of parameters, and two choices are common.

A diagonal covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k = \text{diag}(\sigma_{k1}^2, \sigma_{k2}^2, \ldots, \sigma_{kD}^2)\) means that the features are uncorrelated within each component. It reduces the covariance parameters from \(K \cdot D(D+1)/2\) to \(K \cdot D\). The clusters can still be elliptical, but their axes are aligned with the coordinate axes.

A spherical covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k = \sigma_k^2\mathrm{Id}\) makes each component spherical, with a size \(\sigma_k\) that can differ between components. It reduces the covariance parameters to \(K\). This keeps the probabilistic form of GMMs while approaching the geometric simplicity of K-means. Figure 11.10 compares the three covariance types.

The GMM Likelihood Function

We estimate the parameters by maximum likelihood. For a data set \(\{\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_N\}\) of independent observations the likelihood is \[ L = \prod_{i=1}^N p(\mathbf{x}_i) = \prod_{i=1}^N \left[\sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)\right]. \]Taking the logarithm turns the product into a sum \[ \ln L = \sum_{i=1}^N \ln\left[\sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)\right]. \]

Direct maximization of this log-likelihood is difficult. The sum inside the logarithm creates a complex likelihood surface with many local maxima. The mixture weights, means and covariances also depend on each other, as in K-means, but in a more complex way.

As an example, consider the gradient with respect to one mean vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \ln L}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}_k} &= \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)} \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}_k}\left[\pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)\right]. \end{aligned}\]The vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) appears in both the numerator and the denominator of a complex fraction, so direct optimization is hard. The covariance matrices and the mixture weights are equally hard to find.

11.6 Expectation-Maximization for GMMs

Direct maximization is hard, so we extend the EM algorithm of K-means to GMMs. The idea is the same, since we alternate between estimating the assignments and updating the model parameters.

Introducing Responsibilities

The central quantity is the responsibility of component \(k\) for data point \(\mathbf{x}_i\) \[ \gamma_{ik} = \frac{\pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)}. \]The responsibility \(\gamma_{ik}\) is the posterior probability, given the current parameters, that component \(k\) generated data point \(\mathbf{x}_i\). The responsibility corresponds to the binary assignment variable \(r_{ik}\) of K-means. It is also the expected value of a hidden indicator that is 1 if component \(k\) generated \(\mathbf{x}_i\) and 0 otherwise. This expected value gives the E-step its name.

K-means assignments are 0 or 1, but responsibilities can take any value between 0 and 1. A data point can therefore belong partly to several clusters, which expresses uncertainty in borderline cases. For each data point the responsibilities sum to 1, \(\sum_{k=1}^K \gamma_{ik} = 1\), so the total probability of the point is split among the components.

Outline and Initialization

The EM algorithm for GMMs alternates between two steps, as for K-means, but it works with probabilities instead of discrete assignments.

The algorithm starts from initial values of the parameters \(\{\pi_k\}\), \(\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\}\) and \(\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k\}\). A common choice uses the K-means result for the means, uniform mixture weights and identity covariance matrices. Another choice is to partition the data at random and to compute initial statistics from each partition. We can also choose the initial means with K-means++.

In the E-step we compute the responsibilities \(\gamma_{ik}\) defined above from the current parameter values. They are our current best estimates of which component generated each data point.

In the M-step we treat the responsibilities \(\gamma_{ik}\) as fixed and maximize the responsibility-weighted log-likelihood of the components. Its gradient matches that of \(\ln L\) at the current parameters. With fixed responsibilities, we can optimize each set of parameters independently. The E-step was straightforward, because the responsibilities follow from Bayes’ theorem (Chapter 2). The M-step needs a separate derivation for the means, the covariance matrices and the mixture weights.

Updating the Mean Vectors

We start with the means, which have the most direct geometric meaning. For component \(k\) we look for the mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) that maximizes the log-likelihood when all other parameters are held fixed.

Taking the derivative of \(\ln L\) with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \ln L}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}_k} &= \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)} \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}_k}\left[\pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)\right]. \end{aligned}\]The chain rule and the fact that \((\partial/\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}_k) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k) \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)\) give \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \ln L}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}_k} &= \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k). \end{aligned}\]The fraction is the responsibility \(\gamma_{ik}\), so \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \ln L}{\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}_k} &= \sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k). \end{aligned}\]

Setting this to zero and solving for \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\) gives \[\begin{aligned} \sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k) &= 0 \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik} (\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k) &= 0 \\ \sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik} \mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k \sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik} &= 0. \end{aligned}\] \[ \boldsymbol{\mu}_k = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik} \mathbf{x}_i}{\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik}}. \]The new mean is the weighted average of all data points, with the responsibilities as weights. This generalizes the K-means result, where the hard assignments \(r_{ik} \in \{0,1\}\) are replaced by soft responsibilities \(\gamma_{ik} \in [0,1]\).

The effective number of points assigned to component \(k\) is \[ N_k = \sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik}. \]With this notation the mean update is \[ \boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{\text{new}} = \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik}\mathbf{x}_i. \]

Updating the Covariance Matrices

The covariance update follows the same principle. We want each component’s covariance to reflect the spread of the data points that belong to it, weighted by their responsibilities.

The derivation needs matrix calculus. We differentiate with respect to the precision matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}\), the inverse of the covariance matrix, and then invert the result.

We start from the multivariate Gaussian density \[ \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{D/2}\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma})^{1/2}} \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right). \]Its logarithm is \[ \ln \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}|\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = -\frac{D}{2}\ln(2\pi) - \frac{1}{2}\ln\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) - \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}). \]Since we differentiate with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}\), we write the determinant term with \(\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = 1/\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1})\), which gives \(\ln\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = -\ln\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1})\).

We need two matrix calculus identities \[ \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{A}} \ln\det(\mathbf{A}) = \mathbf{A}^{-1} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{A}} \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^T. \]The derivative with respect to a matrix is the matrix of derivatives with respect to its elements. The first identity holds for a symmetric matrix such as the precision matrix. In one dimension \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{x}\) are numbers \(a\) and \(x\), and the identities read \(\mathrm{d}\ln a/\mathrm{d}a = 1/a\) and \(\mathrm{d}(a x^2)/\mathrm{d}a = x^2\).

Following the pattern of the means we compute \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}} \ln L &= \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)} \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}}\left[\pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)\right]. \end{aligned}\]The chain rule gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}}\left[\pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)\right] = \pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k) \cdot \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}} \ln \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k). \end{aligned}\]The derivative of the logarithm of the Gaussian is \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}} \ln \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k) &= \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}} \left[-\frac{D}{2}\ln(2\pi) + \frac{1}{2}\ln\det(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}) - \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)^T\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)\right] \\ &= \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k - \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)^T. \end{aligned}\]

Substituting back and using the responsibilities gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}} \ln L &= \sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik} \left[\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k - \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)^T\right]. \end{aligned}\]Setting this to zero and solving gives \[\begin{aligned} \sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik} \left[\frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k - \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)^T\right] &= 0 \\ \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k \sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik} - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)^T &= 0. \end{aligned}\] \[ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{\text{new}} = \frac{1}{N_k} \sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{\text{new}})(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{\text{new}})^T. \]The new covariance is the responsibility-weighted sample covariance. It generalizes the usual covariance formula by weighting each data point by how much it belongs to the component.

Updating the Mixture Weights

Finally we derive the update of the mixture weights, which satisfy the constraint \(\sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k = 1\). This needs Lagrange multipliers (Chapter 10), which handle optimization under a constraint.

The Lagrangian is \[ \mathcal{L} = \ln L + \lambda\left(1 - \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k\right), \]where \(\lambda\) is the Lagrange multiplier.

Setting the derivative with respect to \(\pi_k\) to zero gives \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \pi_k} &= \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)} - \lambda = 0. \end{aligned}\]Multiplying both sides by \(\pi_k\) and summing over all components gives \[\begin{aligned} \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)} &= \lambda \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k = \lambda. \end{aligned}\]The left side simplifies, because the inner sum equals 1 for each data point \[\begin{aligned} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^K \frac{\pi_k\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)} = \sum_{i=1}^N 1 = N = \lambda. \end{aligned}\]

Substituting \(\lambda = N\) into the equation for the derivative and multiplying by \(\pi_k\) turns the fraction into \(\gamma_{ik}\), so \[ \sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik} = N \pi_k. \] \[ \pi_k^{\text{new}} = \frac{N_k}{N}. \]The new mixture weight is the average responsibility of component \(k\) over all data points. Components that explain more data points receive larger weights.

The Complete Algorithm

The complete EM algorithm for GMMs has four steps.

  • Initialize the parameters \(\{\pi_k\}\), \(\{\boldsymbol{\mu}_k\}\) and \(\{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k\}\).

  • In the E-step, compute the responsibilities \[ \gamma_{ik} = \frac{\pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^K \pi_j \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\mu}_j, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j)}. \]

  • In the M-step, update the parameters \[\begin{aligned} N_k &= \sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik} \\ \boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{\text{new}} &= \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik}\mathbf{x}_i \\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{\text{new}} &= \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_{i=1}^N \gamma_{ik}(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{\text{new}})(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k^{\text{new}})^T \\ \pi_k^{\text{new}} &= \frac{N_k}{N}. \end{aligned}\]

  • Repeat the E-step and the M-step until convergence.

Figure 11.11 shows two iterations and a third E-step of this algorithm for three components.

Convergence and Local Optima

As for K-means, each iteration of the EM algorithm for GMMs increases the likelihood or leaves it unchanged. We say that the algorithm has converged when the log-likelihood changes by less than a small chosen threshold between two iterations. The algorithm typically converges to a local maximum, which need not be the global maximum, and the final solution depends on the initialization. We therefore run the algorithm several times from different starting points and keep the solution with the highest likelihood. Figure 11.12 shows two runs that end in different solutions.

Initialization matters more for GMMs than for K-means, because the parameter space is larger and the likelihood surface is more complex. A good initial guess, such as the K-means result, helps the algorithm to reach a good solution and speeds up convergence.

11.7 Advantages of Gaussian Mixture Models

GMMs relax the restrictions of K-means and add new uses.

Comparison with K-means

K-means is a special case of a GMM under three restrictions. First, the mixture weights are equal, \(\pi_k = 1/K\). Second, all components have the same spherical covariance, \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k = \sigma^2\mathrm{Id}\). Third, we let \(\sigma^2 \to 0\), which gives the closest center all the responsibility, so \(\gamma_{ik}\) approaches the binary indicator \(r_{ik}\) of K-means. K-means is thus the most constrained version of the GMM.

An important advantage of GMMs is soft assignment. The responsibility \(\gamma_{ik}\) is the probability that data point \(i\) belongs to cluster \(k\). It expresses the uncertainty of the cluster membership.

K-means finds round clusters, because it uses the Euclidean distance. The covariance matrices \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k\) let a GMM fit elongated or tilted clusters. The eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a covariance matrix give the size, shape and orientation of its ellipse (Chapter 10).

A Generative Model

A GMM is a generative model. It describes the probability distribution of the data, so it can do more than assign clusters.

Synthetic data. Once we have fitted a GMM, we can generate new data points that follow the same distribution. We first select a component \(k\) with probability \(\pi_k\) and then draw a sample from \(\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k)\). A GMM fitted to observed stellar parameters can produce mock catalogs of stellar populations that keep the correlations of the data. Such catalogs help to test survey selection functions and to study observational biases.

Outlier detection. A fitted GMM gives the probability density of any data point \(\mathbf{x}_*\) \[ p(\mathbf{x}_*) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_*|\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k). \]Data points that lie far from all cluster centers or in low-density regions are potential outliers. Stars with unusual abundance patterns can indicate unique nucleosynthetic processes, and galaxies with atypical properties can challenge our understanding of galaxy formation. Figure 11.13 shows a density threshold, the 5th percentile of the density of the data, and three outliers below it.

The density tells us how unusual an object is, which goes beyond simple distance-based measures. In astronomy, outliers often represent rare but important objects rather than measurement errors.

Density estimation. A GMM estimates the probability density of the data, even when the density has several peaks, called modes. The estimated density shows where the clusters lie and how the probability is spread through the feature space. This can guide the search for the physical processes that produced the populations. It also shows regions of parameter space that hold few objects.

11.8 Model Selection with Information Criteria

So far we have assumed that the number of clusters \(K\) is known. In practice, choosing \(K\) is difficult. It is an example of model selection, the choice of a model that explains the data well without overfitting.

The elbow method and the silhouette analysis do not use a probability model. A GMM has a likelihood, so we can use the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) and the Akaike information criterion (AIC).

The Model Selection Challenge

As \(K\) increases, the model can fit the data more closely, and the log-likelihood increases. The extra parameters may fit noise instead of real structure.

With \(K=N\), one cluster per data point, the fit is perfect in terms of likelihood, but we learn nothing about the structure of the data. With \(K=1\) the model is as simple as possible, but it fits poorly when the data contain several groups.

Information criteria balance the fit of a model against its complexity. They penalize the likelihood by the number of parameters of the model. They follow the principle of parsimony, often called Occam’s razor. If several models explain the data equally well, we prefer the simplest one. A penalty helps us avoid overfitting.

11.8.1 The Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC)

BIC comes from a Bayesian approach to model selection. We treat the model itself as a variable. Let \(\mathcal{M}_K\) denote a model with \(K\) components. The posterior of the model given the data \(\mathbf{X}\) is \[ p(\mathcal{M}_K|\mathbf{X}) = \frac{p(\mathbf{X}|\mathcal{M}_K)p(\mathcal{M}_K)}{p(\mathbf{X})}. \]

If we have no reason to prefer a model, \(p(\mathcal{M}_K)\) is uniform. The posterior probability is then proportional to the marginal likelihood, or evidence, \(p(\mathbf{X}|\mathcal{M}_K)\) (Chapter 5). The marginal likelihood is the integral over all values of the parameter vector \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_K\), which holds the \(P\) free parameters of \(\mathcal{M}_K\) \[ p(\mathbf{X}|\mathcal{M}_K) = \int p(\mathbf{X}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_K, \mathcal{M}_K)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}_K|\mathcal{M}_K)\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}_K. \]

The marginal likelihood averages the likelihood over the prior. Compare a complex model with many parameters to a simpler one. The complex model spreads its prior probability \(p(\boldsymbol{\theta}_K|\mathcal{M}_K)\) thinly over a large parameter space, because the prior density must integrate to 1. The simpler model concentrates its prior in a smaller region and has a higher density there.

If the complex model does not fit the data much better, its likelihood cannot compensate for the thin prior, so its marginal likelihood is lower. Only if it fits much better over a large part of its parameter space does it overcome this disadvantage. Simple models therefore have a higher marginal likelihood unless the data support more complexity. This is Occam’s razor, built into the integral.

The Laplace Approximation

The marginal likelihood integral generally has no closed form. The Laplace approximation (Chapter 9) approximates the logarithm of the integrand by a quadratic around its maximum \[ \ln[p(\mathbf{X}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_K, \mathcal{M}_K)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}_K|\mathcal{M}_K)] \approx \ln[p(\mathbf{X}|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K, \mathcal{M}_K)p(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K|\mathcal{M}_K)] - \frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_K - \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K)^T \mathbf{A} (\boldsymbol{\theta}_K - \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K). \]Here \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K\) is the maximum of the integrand. The matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is the negative Hessian of the logarithm of the integrand at this point, as in Chapter 9. For large samples the likelihood dominates the prior. Then \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K\) is close to the maximum likelihood estimate, and \(\mathbf{A}\) is approximately the observed information matrix \(\mathcal{I}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K) = -\nabla\nabla \ln p(\mathbf{X}|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K, \mathcal{M}_K)\), which measures how sharply the log-likelihood peaks.

With this Gaussian approximation the integral becomes \[\begin{aligned} p(\mathbf{X}|\mathcal{M}_K) &\approx p(\mathbf{X}|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K, \mathcal{M}_K)p(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K|\mathcal{M}_K) \int \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_K - \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K)^T \mathbf{A} (\boldsymbol{\theta}_K - \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K)\right) \mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{\theta}_K \\ &= p(\mathbf{X}|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K, \mathcal{M}_K)p(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K|\mathcal{M}_K) \cdot (2\pi)^{P/2}\det(\mathbf{A})^{-1/2}. \end{aligned}\]

Deriving the BIC Penalty

To see how \(\det(\mathbf{A})\) depends on \(N\), we start from the log-likelihood, which is a sum over \(N\) independent observations \[ \ln p(\mathbf{X}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_K, \mathcal{M}_K) = \sum_{i=1}^N \ln p(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\theta}_K, \mathcal{M}_K). \]With the prior neglected, \(\mathbf{A}\) is also a sum over \(N\) terms \[ \mathbf{A} = -\nabla\nabla \ln p(\mathbf{X}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_K, \mathcal{M}_K) = -\sum_{i=1}^N \nabla\nabla \ln p(\mathbf{x}_i|\boldsymbol{\theta}_K, \mathcal{M}_K). \]This means that \(\mathbf{A}\) grows linearly with \(N\). We write \(\mathbf{A} = N \cdot \mathcal{J}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K)\), where \(\mathcal{J}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K)\) is the average information matrix per observation.

Scaling a \(P \times P\) matrix by a factor \(N\) scales its determinant by \(N^P\). For the determinant of \(\mathbf{A}\) this gives \[\begin{aligned} \det(\mathbf{A}) &= \det(N \cdot \mathcal{J}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K)) = N^P \cdot \det(\mathcal{J}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K)). \end{aligned}\]

Taking the negative logarithm of the marginal likelihood and multiplying by 2 gives \[\begin{aligned} -2\ln p(\mathbf{X}|\mathcal{M}_K) &\approx -2\ln p(\mathbf{X}|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K, \mathcal{M}_K) - 2\ln p(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K|\mathcal{M}_K) - P\ln(2\pi) + \ln\det(\mathbf{A}) \\ &= -2\ln p(\mathbf{X}|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K, \mathcal{M}_K) - 2\ln p(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K|\mathcal{M}_K) \\ &\quad - P\ln(2\pi) + P\ln(N) + \ln\det(\mathcal{J}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K)). \end{aligned}\]The log-likelihood term \(-2\ln p(\mathbf{X}|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K,\allowbreak \mathcal{M}_K)\) is a sum over the \(N\) data points, so it scales as \(\mathcal{O}(N)\). The penalty term \(P\ln(N)\) scales as \(\mathcal{O}(\ln N)\), which grows much more slowly. The remaining terms are the log-prior \(-2\ln p(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K|\allowbreak\mathcal{M}_K)\), the constant \(-P\ln(2\pi)\) and the determinant term \(\ln\det(\mathcal{J}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K))\). They approach constants as \(N\) grows, so they are \(\mathcal{O}(1)\).

For large \(N\) the log-likelihood term dominates, followed by the penalty term \(P\ln(N)\). The \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) terms are small in comparison. Therefore \[\begin{aligned} -2\ln p(\mathbf{X}|\mathcal{M}_K) &\approx -2\ln p(\mathbf{X}|\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_K, \mathcal{M}_K) + P\ln(N) + \mathcal{O}(1). \end{aligned}\]

We keep the log-likelihood term and the penalty \(P\ln(N)\), and we drop the \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) terms. This gives BIC \[ \text{BIC} = -2\ln(\hat{L}) + P\ln(N). \] Here \(\hat{L}\) is the maximum likelihood of the model, \(P\) is the number of free parameters and \(N\) is the number of data points. The number of free parameters of a GMM depends on the covariance structure. For full covariance matrices in \(D\) dimensions it is \[ P = (K-1) + KD + K\frac{D(D+1)}{2} = K\left(1 + D + \frac{D(D+1)}{2}\right) - 1. \] Diagonal covariance matrices give \(P = (K-1) + KD + KD\), and spherical ones give \(P = (K-1) + KD + K\).

BIC Properties and Interpretation

BIC is consistent. Under regularity conditions, it selects the true model as \(N \to \infty\), if the true model is among the candidates. The penalty \(P\ln(N)\) grows with the sample size, so BIC becomes more demanding as the data set grows. With more data we require stronger evidence for a more complex model.

We select the model with the lowest BIC. For two candidate models \(\mathcal{M}_a\) and \(\mathcal{M}_b\), the difference \(\Delta\text{BIC} = \text{BIC}_a - \text{BIC}_b\) is approximately twice the logarithm of the Bayes factor of \(\mathcal{M}_b\) over \(\mathcal{M}_a\). The Bayes factor is the ratio of the marginal likelihoods of the two models, so \(\Delta\text{BIC}\) measures the evidence for \(\mathcal{M}_b\).

BIC assumes large samples compared with the number of parameters, a well-behaved likelihood and appropriately diffuse priors. In astronomical applications these conditions are not always met, for example with small samples, complex parameter interdependencies or multimodal distributions. BIC is therefore only one piece of evidence, and we must also use scientific knowledge.

11.8.2 The Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)

AIC comes from information theory and estimates how well a model predicts new data. It connects to the entropy and the cross-entropy of Chapter 8. It is based on the Kullback-Leibler divergence, which measures how far the fitted distribution is from the true one. In the coding picture of Chapter 8, this divergence is the extra average code length from using the fitted distribution instead of the true one. Akaike’s idea was to choose the model with the smallest distance to the true data-generating process.

If we use the same data to fit a model and to evaluate it, we overestimate how well the model predicts new data. This optimistic bias grows with the number of parameters, because complex models can fit noise.

Akaike showed that for large \(N\) this bias is about \(P\). We subtract \(P\) from the observed log-likelihood to estimate how well the model predicts new data. Multiplying the result by \(-2\) gives the AIC \[ \text{AIC} = -2\ln(\hat{L}) + 2P. \]

As for BIC, we select the model with the lowest AIC. The AIC penalty \(2P\) is smaller than the BIC penalty \(P\ln(N)\) when \(\ln(N) > 2\). AIC therefore tends to select more complex models than BIC. For Gaussian errors with known variances, \(-2\ln\hat{L}\) equals \(\chi^2\) up to a constant, so AIC is \(\chi^2 + 2P\) up to that constant. A new parameter must therefore lower \(\chi^2\) by more than 2.

For small samples we use the corrected AIC, written \(\text{AIC}_c\). It is defined as \[ \text{AIC}_c = \text{AIC} + \frac{2P(P+1)}{N-P-1}. \]The standard AIC works well for large \(N\) but can be biased when the sample is small compared with the number of parameters. The correction term grows as \(P\) increases or \(N\) decreases, so it penalizes complex models more when data are scarce.

BIC Versus AIC

BIC and AIC follow different views of model selection. BIC assumes that one true model exists among the candidates and searches for it. AIC assumes that all models are approximations and chooses the model that predicts new data best. AIC is efficient. For large \(N\) its choice approaches the smallest expected prediction error among the candidates, even when the true model is not among them.

Figure 11.14 shows both criteria for a mixture with a varying number of components. Both fall while the fit improves and rise when the penalty outweighs the gain in fit.

Practical Application to GMMs

For each \(K\) we fit the GMM with the EM algorithm. The likelihood at convergence is \(\hat{L}\), and we choose the \(K\) with the lowest BIC or AIC. When BIC and AIC agree on the number of components, the choice is well supported. When they disagree, it helps to examine both solutions. The BIC solution typically contains the most prominent, well-separated clusters. The AIC solution can also contain subtler structures that may matter for the scientific question.

BIC and AIC have different aims, so the better criterion depends on the goal of the study. For a first look at the broad population structure, BIC is a good choice, because it selects fewer components. For a detailed study of subpopulations, AIC can help, because it allows more components. Choosing \(K\) resembles choosing the number of principal components in Chapter 10, because both set the complexity of the model.

The M-steps of K-means and of GMMs have closed-form solutions. Complex probabilistic models often have no analytical solution. In Chapter 12 we turn to sampling and Monte Carlo methods for such models.

11.9 Tutorials: Stellar Populations and Quasars

Principal component analysis (PCA) of Chapter 10 summarizes each object by a few coefficients. Clustering adds another summary, the group of each object, and a group can match a physical population. A mixture model also describes the whole distribution of the objects. Two tutorials apply K-means and Gaussian mixture models. The first looks for the stellar populations of a dwarf galaxy, and the second models quasar spectra after dimension reduction. The full tutorials can be found at https://tingyuansen.github.io/statml/ as 11a and 11b.

Populations of a Dwarf Galaxy

Stars keep the composition of the gas that formed them, and supernovae change that gas. Massive stars explode soon after forming and release magnesium and some iron. Type Ia supernovae, explosions of white dwarfs that gain mass from a binary companion, occur much later and release a large amount of iron. If stars form in bursts, these late explosions add iron between bursts, so the magnesium to iron ratio of the gas, [Mg/Fe], falls. The next burst forms stars from this gas, with a higher iron abundance, [Fe/H], and a lower [Mg/Fe] than the last burst. Each burst can therefore leave a group of stars in the plane of [Fe/H] and [Mg/Fe], and the gap between groups marks a quiet period.

We look for these groups in an APOGEE sample of the Sculptor dwarf galaxy. K-means puts each star in the cluster of the nearest of \(K\) centers, as in Figure 11.15a. The elbow of its inertia, the total squared distance to the centers, points to three clusters (Section 11.3). K-means also assumes round clusters of equal weight, each star in one cluster (Section 11.4), so its three clusters in Figure 11.15a have similar sizes. Burst populations can differ in weight and shape and can overlap, so we use a Gaussian mixture model (GMM). Each component describes one population, with a weight and covariance matrix, and each star has a probability of belonging to each (Section 11.5).

A GMM still needs its number of components \(K\), but the likelihood rises as components are added and so does not choose it. We therefore penalize the number of parameters. The Bayesian information criterion (BIC) and the Akaike information criterion (AIC) are two such penalties. BIC penalizes more than AIC does, and more so as the sample grows, so it tends to select fewer components (Section 11.8).

On these stars, BIC selects two broad populations (Figure 11.15b), and AIC, which penalizes less, selects more and smaller ones (Figure 11.15c). BIC gives the coarse picture, and AIC splits it into smaller groups that may be separate bursts or noise. The number of groups to keep therefore depends on the detail that the science needs.

K-means and the mixture model with AIC are consistent with star formation in repeated bursts. Each group would be one burst, and the gaps between the groups would be the quiet periods, so the number of groups counts the bursts. The same recipe applies to any sample whose populations overlap in a plane of properties. A criterion sets the number of groups, and we read it against the science.

A Mixture Model of Quasar Spectra

A mixture can also model a whole distribution of objects, so the second tutorial turns to quasars. A quasar is a supermassive black hole that accretes gas and shines brightly. Its spectrum has a smooth part from the accretion disk and broad emission lines from fast gas near the black hole. The strengths of the lines and the overall slope of the spectrum differ from quasar to quasar. We therefore want a model of the distribution of spectra, that is, which spectra occur and how often, so that we can find unusual ones. The tutorial uses simulated spectra with thousands of wavelengths each.

A GMM can model this distribution, but the parameters of its covariance matrices grow quadratically with the dimension (Section 11.5). One Gaussian component would then need more parameters than there are spectra. Principal components solve this, because each spectrum is the mean spectrum plus a few numbers times the components, as in Figure 11.16a. The mixture then models these numbers, the PCA coefficients, instead of the wavelengths. The explained variance ratio (Section 10.7) guides how many coefficients to keep, and BIC the number of Gaussian components.

Because the mixture describes the whole distribution, it can flag unusual spectra and generate synthetic ones (Section 11.7). The probability density of the coefficients of a spectrum measures how typical it is. The ten spectra of lowest density each leave the band of typical spectra at many wavelengths (Figure 11.16b). Coefficients drawn from the mixture, multiplied by the principal components and added to the mean spectrum, give synthetic spectra (Figure 11.16a). A survey can then follow up unusual spectra and test methods on mock catalogs.

In both tutorials, a criterion and the goal of the study set how many groups or components to keep. Once this number is chosen, a mixture gives a probability model of the population. It answers how typical an object is, which group it most likely joins and what a new sample would look like. These answers let us test a theory of how a population formed against what we observe. The same questions arise for stars, galaxies and transients.

Further Reading

Steinhaus (1956) formulated the division of a set into homogeneous groups, and Pearson (1894) studied mixtures of distributions. Lloyd (1982) gave the iterative algorithm that K-means implementations use. MacQueen (1967) introduced the name K-means. Hartigan and Wong (1979) gave a widely adopted K-means algorithm. Arthur and Vassilvitskii (2007) introduced K-means++, a careful choice of the starting centers. Day (1969) estimated the components of a mixture of normal distributions, and Wolfe (1970) recast clustering as fitting a mixture of multivariate distributions. Dempster et al. (1977) gave the general form of the EM algorithm, a method for maximum likelihood from incomplete data. Redner and Walker (1984) reviewed mixture densities and their maximum likelihood estimation with EM. Titterington et al. (1985) treat the statistical analysis of finite mixtures. Akaike (1974) and Schwarz (1978) developed AIC and BIC, and Bozdogan (1987) extended the theory of AIC. Kaufman and Rousseeuw (1990) give practical guidance on finding groups in data. Dunn (1973) and Bezdek (1981) developed fuzzy c-means, a K-means variant with soft assignments. Selim and Ismail (1984) proved a convergence theorem for K-means type algorithms. Hartigan (1975) is a classic reference on clustering algorithms, and Duda et al. (2001) place them in the field of pattern classification. Ting and Ji (2025) used mixture models to measure bursty star formation in dwarf galaxies, the context and the sample of the first tutorial. Sun et al. (2023) learned a latent factor model of quasar spectra, which generates the spectra of the second tutorial.
